record.name: CardioTrack d.o.o.
record.about:
CardioTrack d.o.o. was founded in 2021 by a small group of engineers and clinicians who spent years watching patients leave cardiology appointments without answers because a standard 24-hour Holter simply wasn't long enough to catch an intermittent arrhythmia. We set out to build something a general practitioner in Novi Sad could hand a patient on a Friday afternoon, knowing that by the following week they would have seven days of continuous ECG data waiting in a structured, readable portal.

Our core product is the CardioTrack patch — a single-use, adhesive ECG monitor worn on the chest for up to seven days. Paired with our clinician portal, it gives cardiologists a timestamped record they can review at their own pace, with automatic flagging of candidate events. We currently supply a handful of private cardiology practices and one outpatient clinic in Vojvodina. The team is twelve people: two biomedical engineers, three firmware and software developers, two quality and regulatory specialists, a clinical liaison, and three people handling operations and sales. We are based at NTP Novi Sad, which gives us access to lab space and keeps us close to the university hospital ecosystem we depend on. What sets us apart is that we built the patch hardware and the clinical software in-house from day one, so we are not dependent on a third-party OEM for either.
products: CardioTrack patch — single-use 7-day adhesive ECG monitor
Clinician portal — web dashboard for reviewing flagged arrhythmia events
Raw data export service — anonymised CSV and EDF exports for research use
Device leasing kit — reusable programmer and patient instruction pack for GP practices
tech: Embedded C (firmware for custom ASIC and Nordic nRF5340 SoC)
Python (signal processing pipeline and ML model training)
AWS (IoT Core, S3, Lambda, RDS PostgreSQL)
JIRA and Confluence for regulatory documentation tracking

challenges.text: Too many false atrial fibrillation alarms when patients move.
challenges.detail:
Our motion artefact problem is straightforward to describe and hard to fix. When a patient moves quickly — walking fast, reaching overhead, rolling over in bed — the electrode contact changes momentarily and the raw signal looks enough like atrial fibrillation that our current classifier flags it. Right now roughly one in four AF alerts that land in the clinician portal turns out to be a motion artefact once the cardiologist looks at the raw trace. That rate is too high; clinicians have told us they are starting to ignore low-confidence flags entirely, which defeats the purpose of automatic detection.

We have a three-axis accelerometer on the patch and we log its data alongside the ECG at 50 Hz, so we have the raw material to do better. Our dataset currently holds about 1,400 completed patient recordings, each tagged by one of two reviewing cardiologists as true AF, other arrhythmia, or noise. The problem is that our two biomedical engineers are occupied with hardware revisions for the next device generation and neither has deep experience with time-series classification beyond what they have read. We have no budget for a large external contract — somewhere in the range of €15,000–25,000 is what we can move without board approval. We need a false-positive rate below ten percent without missing confirmed AF events. A working prototype model integrated into our Python pipeline by the end of 2025 would be a good outcome.

challenges.text: We need a clinical validation study in Serbia before CE marking.
challenges.detail:
CE marking under MDR requires clinical evidence, and for a class IIa active device like ours the notified body has made clear that a post-market clinical follow-up plan is not enough on its own at this stage. We need a prospective study in which patients wear the CardioTrack patch alongside a predicate device simultaneously, and a clinician adjudicates the results. The study needs to be run in Serbia, partly because that is where our existing clinical relationships are and partly because running it abroad would cost more than we can justify before we have revenue to match.

We have a clinical liaison, Milena Ðorić, who has contacts at two private cardiology practices in Novi Sad, but neither practice has experience running a formal clinical investigation under the MDR-aligned Serbian Medical Devices Act framework. We need someone who understands how to write a clinical investigation plan, navigate the ethics committee application, and help us manage data collection in a way that will satisfy our notified body, TÜV SÜD. Target enrolment is around 120 patients over six months. We have set aside roughly €30,000 for the study itself, not including device costs. We need ethics approval and the first patient enrolled before the end of Q1 2026, or our 2027 CE mark timeline slips by at least a year.
